John Chambers writes:
 > S-Plus from Insightful, and R from the R development team, are
 > implementations that differ in details from any of the versions out of
 > Bell Labs (and so they should).  I repeat, this is a good time for
 > positive suggestions for improvements, particularly if they could be
 > incorporated into both systems.
 > 
 > Positive suggestions, preferably.

My positive suggestion would be for the formation of some sort of committee to
draft an ANSI-like set of S Language standards that S-Plus, R and other
implementations could adopt to whatever extent the implementors saw fit. I have
made this suggestion, in private, to people at Insightful and received no
response. 

My *guess* is that the nice folks at Insightful are reluctant to do this
because, in their view, a set of standards that R (along with S-Plus) met would 
only strenghthen R
vis-a-vis S-Plus in the markeplace. But that is only a guess. My personal
opinion is that the opposite is probably true. 

Regards,

Dave Kane

messages.body_plain:
I have a positive suggestion in regards to classes and object oriented
programming in S. It might be a slight overstatement, but I believe the entire S
object model could be based on a 'this' pointer being available in all list
objects. For example, 

        > x <- list(a=1, print = function() {cat('a = ', this$a, '\n')})
        > x$print()
        a = 1
        > x$a <- 4; x$print()
        a = 4

With a feature like this in place, creating classes is no more involved than
creating lists. Class definition would just be object definition, 

        > Aclass <- list(a = 0,
                         init  = function() {this$a <- 0;}, 
                         clone = function() {x <- this; x$init(); return(x)},
                         copy  = function() {return(this)}
                        )

        > xA <- Aclass; yA <- xA$copy(); zA <- yA$clone()
        > ...

Granted this is a loose object model, there would be no enforcement that objects
define particular functions, no invisible calls to functions having special
status (e.g. assign, or print), and inheritance would be more 'has-a' then
'is-a', but I would argue that this is just the type of object model a rapid
development environment like Splus needs.
        In terms of implementation, it should not be too hard. It ought to be
possible to pass a reference as a hidden argument to any function and name it
'this' using existing argument passing machinery, the tricky bit would be
determining which object 'this' should refer to. But with all the frame
information floating around it ought to be doable.
        So that's my suggestion, 

        Matt

messages.subject: Re: recover
messages.body_plain:
My original question:

********************
... what looks like a very useful debugging tool, recover(),
is documented in the Help files and exists in the "main" library. But it
does not seem to work. Does anyone know if this function can be used and, if
so, how it should be invoked? Or is it just another piece of Help system
flotsam?
*********************

My thanks to Terry Therneau and Brian Ripley who informed me that giving
recover as the error function in options, i.e., options(error=recover) , is
the way to invoke this capability. I wish I had known about this some time
ago, as it is a very nice debugging tool.

The closest Help does to explain this is in the documentation on the error
component of options(), which is:

        a function with no arguments that should be called when an error or
interrupt occurs. S-PLUS provides the functions dump.calls and dump.frames
for this purpose; they dump the outstanding function calls and all
associated frames, respectively. For more details, see the help file for
these functions. Setting error=NULL eliminates all error actions.

I have no doubt that this is crystal clear for some; obviously, it was not
for me.

messages.subject: simulation performance problem with SPlus 6.0
messages.body_plain:
To: s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
   From: Gary Sabot <gary at sabot.com>
   Date: Wed, 26 Sep 2001 10:23:01 -0400
   Subject: [S] simulation performance problem with SPlus 6.0
   
   I have been having performance problems involving my simulation
   applications on Splus 6.0, and was hoping some of you might be able
   offer suggestions on how to speed things up.  
   ...
     rowcount  Splus 3.4  Splus 6.0    R
     10          .01        0.16      .01
     100         .13        1.57      .09
     1000       1.29       16.39      .93
     10000      15.54     295.93      8.27

I thought I'd summarize the responses I've received so far.  The root
of the problem is that in Splus 6.0, list subscripting (the '[['
operator) takes time proportional to the length of the list, unlike
previous releases.

John Gavin found a similar slowdown on Splus 6.0.3 on an NT4.

Andrew Sinclair was able to speed up the performance of the benchmark
in Splus 6.0 by a factor of 5 or so, for the problem with 10,000 rows.
This is much better than before, but still much slower than Splus 3.4
or R.  On my machine, in Splus 6.0, 10,000 rows with Andrew's revised
code now takes 63 seconds:

    From: "Sinclair, Andrew (MIP London)"
         <ASinclair at maninvestmentproducts.com>
    To: 'Gary Sabot' <gary at sabot.com>
    Subject: RE: [S] simulation performance problem with SPlus 6.0
    Date: Wed, 26 Sep 2001 16:22:12 +0100
    
    One thing I have tried for this type of problem, with some success, 
    is to use one of the apply/sapply family in conjunction with 
    assign(,frame=0) to pass data from one iteration to the next.
    
    Here's an example for the benchmark you gave - it gives a 
    speed up on my machine (using Splus 5 admittedly) for 
    rowcount=10,000 of 240 -> 56 seconds, an improvement 
    of over 4 times.  Still not as good as your figures for 3.4 though!
    
    benchmark.acs <- function(rowcount=5)
    {
      data <- lapply(1:rowcount,function(x){rnorm(30)})
      ### initialise the previous data (in frame 0)
      assign('prev.results',NA,where=0)
      ### use sapply to loop through the data, get previous results from
      ### frame 0 and re-store them when finished
      results.at.each.iter <- sapply(data, function(idata){
        ### may not even need the get() here
        ans <- benchmark.2(get('prev.results',where=0),idata)  
        assign('prev.results',ans,where=0)   
        ans
      })
      results.at.each.iter
    }

Steve Weller at Insightful had a different workaround; it used unlist
to exploit a property of the benchmark that is not true of my overall
application, which has dataframes rather than vectors as the elements
of the list.  Still it is an interesting technique.  This code takes
66 seconds for 10,000 rows on Splus 6.0:

   benchmark.nolist <-
   function(rowcount)
   {
           new.result <- rep(0, rowcount)
           data <- unlist(lapply(1:rowcount, function(x)
           {
                   rnorm(30)
           }
           ))
           temp.result <- sum(data[1:30]) + 1
           counter <- 1
           while(rowcount > 0) {
                   new.result[counter] <- temp.result
                   counter <- counter + 1
                   if((new.result[counter - 1] > 4) | (new.result[counter - 1] 
< 20 )) {
          temp.result <- sum(data[((counter-1)*30+1):(counter*30)]) +           
    ifelse(is.na(new.result[counter - 1]), 1, new.result[counter-1])
                   } else {
                        cat("B:", rowcount, "\n")
                        temp.result <- sum(data) *new.result[counter-1]
                   }
                   new.result[counter] <- temp.result
                   rowcount <- rowcount - 1
           }
           new.result
   }
   
Finally, David Smith at Insightful indicates that they plan to address
this list subscripting performance problem in S-Plus 6.1.

--gary

Original message:
------------------
From: Gary Sabot <gary at sabot.com>
Message-ID: <15281.58565.324381.609970 at delphioutpost.com>
Date: Wed, 26 Sep 2001 10:23:01 -0400
To: s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
Subject: simulation performance problem with SPlus 6.0

I have been having performance problems involving my simulation
applications on Splus 6.0, and was hoping some of you might be able
offer suggestions on how to speed things up.  I've been developing and
using these applications for years with SPlus 3.4, and recently
switched over to Splus 6.0 on faster hardware.  Now that much of my
application has been ported (which other than the [.data.frame issue
was pretty straighforward), it works correctly, but unfortunately it
is significantly slower.

I have abstracted the portions of the simulation that slowed down the
most into a short benchmark, below.  For rowcount=10000 it takes about
15 seconds in Splus 3.4, 8 seconds in R, and 295 seconds in Splus 6.0.

For an earlier version of this benchmark, Insightful support had
suggested that there might be a performance issue involving how
reference counting is done in the new S engine (see below), but I
haven't heard anything beyond that.

I don't mean to suggest that Splus 6.0 is slower than Splus 3.4 in
general; it simply is the case that the mix of capabilities used by my
simulation applications happen to have slowed down.  So for obvious
reasons, I'm focusing on describing that problem area in this message,
in hopes of finding a solution.  I certainly have seen vectorized
calculations speed up in Splus 6.0 relative to 3.4.  In some cases the
speed up is only available at larger vector sizes (which is generally
where you would think performance matters most), with small vector
sizes unable to fully amortize the increased overhead.  So vectorized
operations on small vectors can run slower in Splus 6.0.  This can be
a problem if the small vector manipulation is inside the inner loop of
a larger non-vectorizable simulation...

----------------
DETAILS:

My application is basically a loop doing a financial simulation, where
the calculation of iteration n+1 can depend on possibly everything
that has happened before that point in the simulation, or perhaps only
a recent window of several iterations of history.  So I do not think
the loop can be vectorized.  Other application characteristics that
might be important: Splus 3.4 encouraged you when tuning your code to
move the body of the simulation loop to a separate function leaving
behind as little as possible, which could improve garbage collection
as the inner function would reclaim some space each time it exited.
Also, the enclosing data structure is a often list whose elements are
dataframes, or occasionally lists of dataframes.  The number of rows
is large (number of time periods), but the number of columns is fixed
(data needed at each iteration).  In the benchmark below, the elements
are simply vectors.

Many of these characteristics would likely be common to many types of
simulation code, not only financial industry investment strategy
simulations.

Benchmark function:

benchmark.1 <- function(rowcount=5)
{
  #load in/initialize the simulation data.  In the general case, each
  # element of the list might be a dataframe, i.e. with securities as
  # rows and security characteristics as columns.  The number of
  # characteristics is generally fixed, but the number of securities
  # can vary and be large, i.e. thousands.  However, in this benchmark,
  # each elemetn is simply a vector of 30 random numbers.
  data <- lapply(1:rowcount,function(x){rnorm(30)})

  #At end, this vector the results of each iteration.
  #There can be thousands or more iterations, depending on the 
  #granularity of the time period.  And in the general case, 
  #The result might resemble the input in structure, i.e. a list
  #whose elements are dataframes, each processed version of the corresponding
  #input dataframe and its predecessors.
  results.at.each.iter <- rep(NA,rowcount)

  for(i in 1:rowcount) {
#could be this
#     results.at.each.iter <- benchmark.2(i,results.at.each.iter,data)
# But lets say for simplicity that it is this simpler call
# which just passes a single1 time period, or at worst a window of several 
recent
# time periods, but not all of them:
     results.at.each.iter[i] <- 
benchmark.2(results.at.each.iter[max(i-1,1)],data[[i]])
  }
  results.at.each.iter
}

benchmark.2 <- function(prev.result,data)
{
  #any arbitrary calculation might be here, so don't 
  #take advantage of the simplicity of this benchmark
  #would likely return a vector with length equal to the number of 
  #securities, but here I just return one number.
  if(is.na(prev.result) | (prev.result>4) | (prev.result<20)) {
    new.result <- sum(data,na.rm=T)+ ifelse(is.na(prev.result),1,prev.result)
  } else {
    new.result <- sum(data)*prev.result
  }
  new.result
}

----------------
All timings below are in seconds.  Splus 3.4 is on a slower machine,
an Ultra60 360 mhz/2 CPU/512K RAM.  Both R and SPlus 6.0 are on an
E250 400 mhz/2CPU/2 Gig RAM).  Timings done by
unix.time(benchmark.1(rowcount)):

  rowcount  Splus 3.4  Splus 6.0    R
  10          .01        0.16      .01
  100         .13        1.57      .09
  1000       1.29       16.39      .93
  10000      15.54     295.93      8.27

The behavior for Splus 6 on this example is around ten times worse
than it used to be with SPlus 3.4 for small numbers, and then gets
worse for larger numbers (i.e. quadratic behavior?)

----------------
Finally, here is my summary of two possible explanations from
Insightful, from when they responded concerning an earlier, different
version of this benchmark (so it is certainly possible that the
explanation does not accurately apply to this benchmark with my new
changes; in that case, the error is mine):

   1. When S Version 4 first came out, when a program did this:

        List[[i]] <- newValue

   it first incremented the reference count on List (including all of its
   elements, so this is expensive), then it updates List[[i]], then it
   decrements the ref count on List (again expensive).  SPlus 6.0 may
   still be doing this.  

   2. A secondary effect (a linear effect) is that more functions
   use the somewhat slower new method dispatch system of SV4.
   (More functions are generic and more use the new system --
   both slow things a bit.)  One can use the el() function instead
   of "[[" to speed things up since it is not generic (hence
   only works with numeric subscripts). 

--gary

Missing Values

Everybody has them, nobody wants them

More often than not empirical researchers are confronted by an 
abundance of missing values. As the phenomenon is usually not seen 
as a possible threat to the validity of the research, the most 
common approach to this problem is simply to deny it.  The 4% to 5% 
missing values in a few variables in a small part of the data under 
research do not seem that important. However, when one looks closer 
at the  'important' variables in the data set, percentages of 
missing values of 30% to 70% are not uncommon. Now this would not be 
a problem if Fate dropped these blind spots all over the responses. 
The adequate action then would be to simply enlarge the sample and 
use only the known values. All statistical packages provide this 
simple escape route.

Alas, Fate is not as blind as the old Greek let us believe. Just as, 
in former days, whole families were struck by disasters, nowadays 
SES-classes or age-classes or other minorities are 
disproportionately struck by missing values. If within those classes 
Fate is turning a blind eye, truth can still be found using 
ML-methods (e.g. the EM-algorithm) or simulating a few complete data 
sets from the single incomplete set (Multiple Imputation). The last 
25 years have seen a rapid development of algorithms, but these are 
only slowly being applied in statistical software.

Sometimes, Fate is not striking blind at all. The highest income 
appears to be unknown. Populations high at risk refuse to be sampled 
for blood, and in longitudinal clinical research most missing values 
are found for patients in the worst health conditions. In 
agricultural data, highly productive cows no longer show milk yields 
due to an illness correlated with productivity. But laboratories 
have their share as well, the lowest values being undetectable, the 
highest putting the instruments on ERROR. In short, in this 
situation the missing value depends on the true, but unknown, value 
of the variable itself.

Missing values can really be a threat to your research. This one-day 
conference may help you to deal effectively with this problem.

messages.subject: rmvnorm with non-positive matrix
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus Users,

I am trying to randomly sample from a multivariate normal distribution whose
covariance matrix is apparently somewhat non-positive.  I understand that this
suggests some "collinearity" in a subset of the random variables, but don't
quite see why that would preclude a defensible random sampling procedure.
Applying rmvnorm causes a stop error owing to the non-positive matrix.  So on
the surface rmvnorm would not work for this case.

Some co-workers had previously sampled from this same multivariate normal
distribution using a Choleski decomposition approach.   I tried this same
approach and got the following warning when applying the Chol() function

     Warning messages:
       Warning in chol(covmat): Choleski decomposition not of full rank

I persevered and ignored this warning, completed the procedure to obtain a
result.   I worried that the result,
may not be defensible (given the warning ... which I'm unable to properly
interpret).  So my question is whether
the Choleski approach is defensible in this case.  And if not what is the
recommended approach is
(for sampling in the case of a non-positive covariance
matrix).

Thanks for any insight you can offer!
Kevin

Congratulations.  You are about 1/3 of the way toward reinventing Smalltalk.
Of course, if you really want to do object oriented programming, you could
save the time and trouble of trying to redesign R and S by just learning
Smalltalk.  They (the Smalltalk community) have been thinking and programming
nothing but objects for over 20 years, and it shows.

>>>>> "M" == Matt Calder <calder at phz.com> writes:

  M>    I have a positive suggestion in regards to classes and object oriented
  M> programming in S. It might be a slight overstatement, but I believe the
  M> entire S object model could be based on a 'this' pointer being available
  M> in all list objects. For example,

  >> x <- list(a=1, print = function() {cat('a = ', this$a, '\n')}) x$print()
  M>         a = 1
  >> x$a <- 4; x$print()
  M>         a = 4

  M> With a feature like this in place, creating classes is no more involved
  M> than creating lists. Class definition would just be object definition,

  >> Aclass <- list(a = 0,
  M>                     init = function() {this$a <- 0;}, clone = function() 
{x <-
  M> this; x$init(); return(x)}, copy = function() {return(this)} )

  >> xA <- Aclass; yA <- xA$copy(); zA <- yA$clone() ...

  M> Granted this is a loose object model, there would be no enforcement that
  M> objects define particular functions, no invisible calls to functions
  M> having special status (e.g. assign, or print), and inheritance would be
  M> more 'has-a' then 'is-a', but I would argue that this is just the type of
  M> object model a rapid development environment like Splus needs. In terms
  M> of implementation, it should not be too hard. It ought to be possible to
  M> pass a reference as a hidden argument to any function and name it 'this'
  M> using existing argument passing machinery, the tricky bit would be
  M> determining which object 'this' should refer to. But with all the frame
  M> information floating around it ought to be doable. So that's my
  M> suggestion,

  M>    Matt

  >> John Chambers writes: S-Plus from Insightful, and R from the R
  >> development team, are implementations that differ in details from any of
  >> the versions out of Bell Labs (and so they should). I repeat, this is a

  >> could be incorporated into both systems. Positive suggestions,
  >> preferably.

messages.subject: lme convergence problem [summary and con'td]
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Renaud Lancelot and Charles C. Berry  for their help
with my problem with lme() convergence. To summarize my previous
question and the replies I have received as well as to ask
a follow-up question, I will reframe my initial inquiry.

My experimental design has one experimental factor (SeqPos, fixed effect,
4 levels) and one blocking factor (seq, random effect, 6 levels) and eight
replications.

I want to estimate the statistical significance of the random effec bi by
comparing
                eijk = betaj + bi + eijk:
with
                yijk = betaj + eijk where 
where betaj is the fixed effect, bi~Norm(0,sigma.b^2) and
eijk~Norm(0,sigma^2).

To that end, I tried to fit the two following models:

fit1<-lme(Targ~SeqPos,random=~1|seq, data=data) --> FALSE CONVERGENCE
fit2<-lme(Targ~SeqPos,random=pdIdent(~1), data=data) --> SINGULAR CONVERGENCE

and use anova(fit1,fit2).

Charles C. Berry and Renaud Lancelot pointed out to me that the lme()
function 
could probably not fit the second model (and that my syntax was probably
wrong): I needed to use gls() or lm() to fit the second model (see below).

I still have a problem understanding why the first fit indicates
FALSE CONVERGENCE. With respect to this issue, Renaud Lancelot wrote:

>The kind of message you get indicates that the likelihood function is
>very flat and that the algorithm cannot find a minimum. For example, if
>you have a random-intercept model, it might indicate that there is no
>within-group correlation (lack of structure related to the group in this
>particular dataset), or that many groups have a very low number of
>individuals (diseased design).

Interestingly, the following fit - which is equivalent to fit1 - seems to 
converge without problem:

fit3<-gls(Targ~SeqPos,correlation=corCompSymm(form=~1|seq),data=data)

What is FALSE CONVERGENCE? What parameters should I change in lmeControl()
to make lme() converge? I tried a few without success. What should I look
at to see whether my dataset presents some of the characteristics that
Renaud Lancelot describes (see also below for a summary of my data set).
If the problem is related to the fact that the random effect does not
seem to be statistically different from zero, why is lme() unable to
give me that answer while gls() can?

Thank you for your help,

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

#------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, Charcles C. Berry suggested:

fit.lme <- lme(Targ ~ SeqPos, random = ~ 1 | seq, data = data)
fit.lm <- lm(Targ ~ SeqPos, data = data)
anova(fit1.lme,fit2.lm)

Renaud Lancelot (I summarize/adapt his response hopefully without
introducing any error of my part) indicated that these two models 
were equivalent:

fit.lme<-lme(Targ~SeqPos,random=~1|seq,data=data)
fit.gls.1<-gls(Targ~SeqPos, correlation=corCompSymm(form = ~1|seq ),
        data = data)

and that I could test the random effect by using 

fit.gls.2 <- gls(Targ ~ SeqPos, correlation = NULL, data = data)
anova(fit.gls.1,fit.gls.2)
       Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test      L.Ratio    p-value 
fit.gls.1     1  6 771.3564 790.7750 -379.6782       
fit.gls.2     2  5 769.6687 785.8509 -379.8344 1 vs 2   0.3123263  0.5763

since fit.gls.2 fits the same model as fit.lm (this analysis suggests
that the random effect is not statistically different from zero).
Alternatively, one could also look at the interval of confidence of bi 
with the function intervals().

Note that both approaches works well with the Machine/Worker dataset
defined in Pinheiro's book.

messages.subject: Summary: Problems with "assign" in S+6
messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon,

the only two replies I got for my message were to ask to forward replies.
>From that I concluded that some other folks are also experiencing some
difficulties to switch to S+6.  I finally found out by myself what was
happening.  Here it is for the ones interested:

You probably noticed that the code I posted this morning, see at the end of
this message, mimicked the code of the Splus 6 Programmer's Guide
p.580-581.  But as it is this code will not work and it is not easy --- for
me anyway --- to find out why; documentation of the "library" function ---
or any other related function --- will not help.  The "Green book", J.
Chambers, spells it out on page 218: "The status of databases when attached
is either 'read' or 'readwrite'.  In particular, library ALWAYS attaches
databases readonly."  Using "attach", instead of "library", with the new
"pos" argument will attach the requested database with 'readwrite' status;
an alternate solution is to still use "library" and then "setDBStatus(where
= whatever name or position, writable = 'readwrite')".  Should one approach
be favored?  I leave the answer to more knowlegeable users to comment.

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat

télecopieur          : (418) 835-6657

messages.subject: behavior of unpaste
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-news,

I was playing with unpaste(), and thought the following behaviour is not
intuitive nor consistent:

> unpaste("", ",")
Problem in rep.int: rep() only defined for length(times)
==1 or length(x): rep.int(1:n, times) 
Use traceback() to see the call stack

> unpaste("ABC", ",")
[[1]]:
[1] "ABC"

In the first case, I would have expected a return value of character(0)
instead of the cryptic error message.  (OK, actually I used strsplit in R
and found unpaste to be the nearest thing to it in Splus.  This desired
behaviour is what strsplit does.)

System:  Splus 6.0.3 on WinNT.

Cheers,
Andy

messages.subject: Summary on generating random data from dist. with 0 skewness andsome kurtosis
messages.subject_clean: Summary on generating random data from dist. with 0 skewness andsome kurtosis
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all for considering my problem about generating random data 
from distributions with zero skewness and some kurtosis values.  Here 
are some tricks to do that : 

1.  from Dr. Luciano Molinari <luciano.molinari at kispi.unizh.ch>

A simple way could be:
------------
zzz_rnorm(1000)
sign(zzz)*abs(zzz)^alfa
--------------
for some alfa.

2.  from Dirk Eddelbuettel <edd at debian.org> 

We could try a mixture of normals -- ie flip a coin (use a uniform with
some cutoff c where 0 < c < 1 ) to choose between N(0, sigma_1) and N
(0,sigma_2). 

3.  from David Parkhurst <parkhurs at indiana.edu> 

This seems to work:
x1<- rlnorm(500,log(100),0.5)  # Skewed to right
x2<- rlnorm(500,log(100),0.5)  # Skewed to right
mu<- exp(log(100)+0.5^2/2)  # mean of the log-normal distribution
x2<- mu-(x2-mu)   # Skew this distribution to the left
x<- c(x1,x2)    # Combine the two distributions
plot(density(x))  # Check the result
qqnorm(x)

4.  from Rosenfeld, Simon (NCI) <rosenfes at mail.nih.gov> 

Zillion of methods: take for example student's t-distribution,
cauchy or laplace

5.  from Greg Snow <snow at fisher.byu.edu>

Take a look at the "rstab" function, it may be just what we want.

6.  from David L Lorenz <lorenz at usgs.gov> 

His guess is that we want a distribution with positive skewness.  The t
distribution will do this.  Use the rt function to generate random 
variates for any number of degrees of freedom.  The larger the df, the 
nearer normal.

7.  from Matt Kurbat <Matt.Kurbat at kmv.com

We can use a mixture of normals distribution.  Our density will be a 
weighted average of two normal densities (same mean, different 
variances).  
By varying the parameters of the normals, and the proportion allocated
to each, we can achieve the desired result.
Venables and Ripley (Modern Applied Statistics) discuss normal
mixtures.

8.  from jonathan david norton <jdnorton at midway.uchicago.edu> 

Generate normals, square them, put the original sign back  on. This
distribution is symmetrical and has extremely heavy tails.

9.  from Tom Jagger <tjagger at insightful.com> 

We can use the t distribution it has skewness and mean 0. 
Use rt(n,df) where the degrees of freedom can be any positive real 
number!

10.  from Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU 

An easy way to do this is to use a mixture of two normal distributions, 
one of which has much bigger variance than the other, for example

y <- ifelse(runif(10000) < 0.95, rnorm(10000, sd = 1), rnorm(10000, sd 
= 5))

We can adjust the degree of kurtosis by adjusting either the mixture
probabilies or the standard deviation of one of the components.

11.  from Bob Wheeler <bwheeler at echip.com>

We can use the Johnson system. See the SuppDists package.

Abdul Kudus
======================
Dept. of Statistics
Bandung Islamic University
Indonesia
======================

          **********************************************

INTRODUCTION
============

The 2001 WI/IAT Joint Conference provides an international forum for
sharing original research results and practical development
experiences among researchers and application developers from all Web
Intelligence and Intelligent Agent Technology related areas.

287 full papers coming from 39 countries and regions of all continents
and touching a wide spectrum of topics related to both theory and
applications were submitted to WI-2001 and IAT-2001.  Out of them 53
papers were selected for regular presentations (20 minutes for each
presentation) and 85 for short presentations (15 minutes for each
presentation).  The 2001 WI/IAT Joint Conference encourages both new
theory/methodologies and real-world applications, and covers broad and
diverse topics in Web Intelligence and Intelligent Agent Technology.

The technical sessions include: Web Information System Environment and
Foundations; Web Human-Media Engineering; Web Information Management;
Web Information Retrieval; Web Agents; Web Mining and Farming;
Web-Based Applications; Web-Based Active Contents; Advanced Topics and
New Methodologies; Formal Agent Theories; Agent Computational
Architecture and Infrastructure; Agent Learning and Adaptation;
Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining Agents; Distributed Intelligence;
Business Agent Solutions; Agent-Based Applications; as well as a Demo
Session including about 20 system demoes.

The joint conference program is enriched by two keynote speakers:
Edward A. Feigenbaum and Benjamin Wah, and ten (10) invited speakers:
Nick Cercone, James Hendler, W. Lewis Johnson, Riichiro Mizoguchi,
Prabhakar Raghavan, Patrick S. P. Wang, Toyoaki Nishida, Zbigniew
W. Ras, Andrzej Skowron, and Katia Sycara.

The conference proceedings are published by Springer-Verlag for
WI-2001 and World Scientific for IAT-2001 as books, entitled "Web
Intelligence: Research and Development" (LNAI 2198), and "Intelligent
Agent Technology: Research and Development", respectively.

The conference will organize a tour during the conference to Ikaho hot
spring resort area, one of the most famous hot springs areas in Japan,
and have a banquet at Kogure Hotel in Ikaho as well as a reception at
Rinko-kaku that is a traditional Japanese guest house constructed in
1884.

We are very grateful to the WI-2001 and IAT-2001 sponsors: ACM SIGART,
Maebashi Institute of Technology, Maebashi Convention Bureau, Maebashi
City Government, Gunma Prefecture Government, The Japan Research
Institute, Limited, US AFOSR/AOARD, AROFE, and Web Intelligence
Laboratory, Inc. for their generous support. We thank ACM SIGWEB,
SIGCHI, Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence, JSAI SIGFAI,
SIGKBS, and IEICE SIGKBSE for being in cooperation with the conference.

Note: The organizers of WI-2001 and IAT-2001 appreciate receiving many
good suggestions with respect to renaming both conferences.  In the
light of the representation, scope, and quality of the accepted papers
as well as the very positive response from internatoinal WI and IAT
communities, the organizers have decided to adopt the suggestions and
to rename both conferences into the present titles, from now onward.

messages.subject: pitfall in masking stderr() in S-PLUS 6
messages.subject_clean: pitfall in masking stderr() in S-PLUS 6
messages.body_plain:
This is just a caution of a pitfall that perhaps may save someone's time.

Using S-PLUS 6 Release 2 under NT 4 Service Pack 6, I carelessly (in
multiple ways) defined a utility function in my working .Data:

stderr <- function(x) { stdev(x) / sqrt(length(x)) }

This masked the stderr() function defined in SV4 as part of its connections
suite of functions. I ignored the standard "masked" warning.

When I called my homegrown stderr() within a larger function and tried to
use browser.default() for debugging, 

* browser was entered and then exited immediately;
* The system option for errors was silently set to NULL from dump.calls

Looking at the body of browser.default() under S-PLUS 6, some snippets there
reveal:

if(!exists("old.error", frame = sys.nframe())) {
# effectively, a test for first-time call (vs restart after error)
        old.error <- options(error = NULL, interrupt = NULL)
        on.exit(options(old.error)) 

# deleted 
}

and

cat(message, "\n", file = "|stderr")

and

stdErr <- stderr()

amongst other uses of |stderr and stderr() .

These constructs were not present in S-PLUS 2000 and as far as I know,
earlier versions of S-PLUS. 

The easy and proper workaround, of course, is to rename my function to
something that does not mask stderr(), such as stnderr(). 

So perhaps the moral of the story is that masking system functions is to be
avoided more so now than ever...

Best Regards,
Bill
----------------------------------------

messages.subject: Re: S4 classes and methods
messages.body_plain:
Matt Calder <calder at phz.com> writes:

>       I have a positive suggestion in regards to classes and object
> oriented programming in S. It might be a slight overstatement, but I
> believe the entire S object model could be based on a 'this' pointer
> being available in all list objects. For example,
> 
>       > x <- list(a=1, print = function() {cat('a = ', this$a, '\n')})
>       > x$print()
>         a = 1
>       > x$a <- 4; x$print()
>         a = 4
> 
> With a feature like this in place, creating classes is no more
> involved than creating lists. Class definition would just be object
> definition,
> 
>       > Aclass <- list(a = 0,
>                        init  = function() {this$a <- 0;}, 
>                        clone = function() {x <- this; x$init(); return(x)},
>                        copy  = function() {return(this)}
>                       )
> 
>       > xA <- Aclass; yA <- xA$copy(); zA <- yA$clone()
>       > ...
> 
> Granted this is a loose object model, there would be no enforcement
> that objects define particular functions, no invisible calls to
> functions having special status (e.g. assign, or print), and
> inheritance would be more 'has-a' then 'is-a', but I would argue
> that this is just the type of object model a rapid development
> environment like Splus needs.
> ...
> [snip]

If S did have a standard and if that standard did not include these
sorts of features that would not imply that you were forbidden from
using them.  S is sufficiently powerful that you can implement
language extensions yourself.  The following code goes a long
way---maybe all the way---toward doing what the above describes.

  this <-
    function()
  {
    x <- deparse(eval(expression(match.call()), local = sys.parent(1)))
    p <- regexpr('\\$', x) - 1
    if(p > 0)
      eval(parse(text = substring(x, 1, p)),
           local = sys.parent(2))
  }

  x <- list(a = 1,
            print = function() cat('a = ', this()$a, '\n', sep = ''))

  Aclass <- list(a = NULL,
                 init = function() {
                   self <- this()
                   self$a <- 0
                   return(self)},
                 clone = function() {return(this()$init())},
                 copy  = function() {return(this())})

All this is very informal and probably fails in situations that I
haven't thought of yet, but the point is that someone who was
motivated could fix it up or implement something similar.

As I understand it a standards body has mainly a sort of
legal/administrative function.  They have to pick and choose among
existing solutions, make precise definitions, and draw up a contract
that describes just what an implementor has to implement.  You
couldn't blame them for ignoring new ideas that nobody in the S
community was using, especially since this "message passing" style of
object methodology goes totally against the grain of the "generic
function" style that the S developers have been implementing for the
last 10 or 11 years.

It's not obvious that S needs an entirely different object model but
if someone starts using one and the idea catches on then maybe after 5
years or so after people have gotten sufficient experience it would
make sense to worry about formalizing it.

-- 
Ed Kademan              508.651.3700
PHZ Capital Partners    508.653.1745 (fax)
321 Commonwealth Road   <kademan at phz.com>
Wayland, MA 01778

messages.subject: Summary: Error in Integrate Function
messages.body_plain:
Four weeks ago I sent out a question regarding the use of the integrate
function.  I was using S-Plus 2000 Release 2 under Windows 98.  Using
S-Plus 2000 Release 3 the problem persists.  I would like to thank Bob
Baskin for his reply and for providing a solution.

Below is a short form of my original message and Bob's reply.

I am running some simulations where I perform the following
transformation. 

x <- abs(rnorm(2000,0,30)) 

x.new <- ifelse(x <= quantile(x, c(0.90)), 0, 0 + (x - quantile(x,
c(0.90)))^2) 

Using this transformation x.new is a linear/quadratic function of x. I
want to get the expected value of x.new given that the original
distribution before any transformations were done came from a normal
distribution with population mean = 0 and standard deviation = 30. To do
this I have been using the following code

> integrand_function(x)
{
        mu <- 0
        sd <- 30
        cut <- qnorm(0.95, 0, sd)
        ifelse(abs(x) <= cut, 0, 1) * (abs(x) - cut)^2 * dnorm(x, mu,
sd)     #
}

> integrate(integrand,-Inf,Inf)[1:4]
$integral:
[1] 4.419641e-008

$abs.error:
[1] 8.737916e-008

$subdivisions:
[1] 1

$message:
[1] "normal termination"

The result of the integrate function is wrong.  It should be 28.14145.

Bob's reply was

i think you have created an integrand that fools integrate() into
thinking it has converged when it hasn't even gotten close to the heart
of the matter.  your function is zero on a long interval.  you know your
function should be zero between -cut and cut (where you have defined cut
to be qnorm(percentile, mu, sigma).  if you integrate over the interval
(cut,inf) (and multiply by two) instead of on the interval (-inf,inf), i
think integrate() will handle your problem.

Using Bob's suggestion works

> integrate(integrand,qnorm(.95,0,30),Inf)[1:4]
$integral:
[1] 14.07073

$abs.error:
[1] 0.000927482

$subdivisions:
[1] 7

$message:
[1] "normal termination"

> 2*unlist(integrate(integrand,qnorm(.95,0,30),Inf)[1])
 integral 
 28.14145

This is the correct answer.

messages.subject: summary on random data with zero skew and some kurtosis
messages.subject_clean: summary on random data with zero skew and some kurtosis
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all for considering my problem about generating random data 
from distributions with zero skewness and some kurtosis values.  Here 
are some tricks to do that : 

1.  from Dr. Luciano Molinari <luciano.molinari at kispi.unizh.ch>

A simple way could be:
------------
zzz_rnorm(1000)
sign(zzz)*abs(zzz)^alfa
--------------
for some alfa.

2.  from Dirk Eddelbuettel <edd at debian.org> 

We could try a mixture of normals -- ie flip a coin (use a uniform with
some cutoff c where 0 < c < 1 ) to choose between N(0, sigma_1) and N
(0,sigma_2). 

3.  from David Parkhurst <parkhurs at indiana.edu> 

This seems to work:
x1<- rlnorm(500,log(100),0.5)  # Skewed to right
x2<- rlnorm(500,log(100),0.5)  # Skewed to right
mu<- exp(log(100)+0.5^2/2)  # mean of the log-normal distribution
x2<- mu-(x2-mu)   # Skew this distribution to the left
x<- c(x1,x2)    # Combine the two distributions
plot(density(x))  # Check the result
qqnorm(x)

4.  from Rosenfeld, Simon (NCI) <rosenfes at mail.nih.gov> 

Zillion of methods: take for example student's t-distribution,
cauchy or laplace

5.  from Greg Snow <snow at fisher.byu.edu>

Take a look at the "rstab" function, it may be just what we want.

6.  from David L Lorenz <lorenz at usgs.gov> 

His guess is that we want a distribution with positive skewness.  The t
distribution will do this.  Use the rt function to generate random 
variates for any number of degrees of freedom.  The larger the df, the 
nearer normal.

7.  from Matt Kurbat <Matt.Kurbat at kmv.com

We can use a mixture of normals distribution.  Our density will be a 
weighted average of two normal densities (same mean, different 
variances).  
By varying the parameters of the normals, and the proportion allocated
to each, we can achieve the desired result.
Venables and Ripley (Modern Applied Statistics) discuss normal
mixtures.

8.  from jonathan david norton <jdnorton at midway.uchicago.edu> 

Generate normals, square them, put the original sign back  on. This
distribution is symmetrical and has extremely heavy tails.

9.  from Tom Jagger <tjagger at insightful.com> 

We can use the t distribution it has skewness and mean 0. 
Use rt(n,df) where the degrees of freedom can be any positive real 
number!

10.  from Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU 

An easy way to do this is to use a mixture of two normal distributions, 
one of which has much bigger variance than the other, for example

y <- ifelse(runif(10000) < 0.95, rnorm(10000, sd = 1), rnorm(10000, sd 
= 5))

We can adjust the degree of kurtosis by adjusting either the mixture
probabilies or the standard deviation of one of the components.

11.  from Bob Wheeler <bwheeler at echip.com>

We can use the Johnson system. See the SuppDists package.

Abdul Kudus
======================
Dept. of Statistics
Bandung Islamic University
Indonesia
======================

> -----Original Message-----
> From: Abdul Kudus [mailto:akudus at stat.unisba.ac.id]
> Sent: Wednesday, October 03, 2001 9:15 PM
> To: S-news at wubios.wustl.edu
> Subject: [S] summary on random data with zero skew and some kurtosis
> 
> 
> Thanks to all for considering my problem about generating random data 
> from distributions with zero skewness and some kurtosis values.  Here 
> are some tricks to do that : 
> 
> 1.  from Dr. Luciano Molinari <luciano.molinari at kispi.unizh.ch>
> 
> A simple way could be:
> ------------
> zzz_rnorm(1000)
> sign(zzz)*abs(zzz)^alfa
> --------------
> for some alfa.
> 
> 2.  from Dirk Eddelbuettel <edd at debian.org> 
> 
> We could try a mixture of normals -- ie flip a coin (use a 
> uniform with
> some cutoff c where 0 < c < 1 ) to choose between N(0, sigma_1) and N
> (0,sigma_2). 
> 
> 
> 3.  from David Parkhurst <parkhurs at indiana.edu> 
> 
> This seems to work:
> x1<- rlnorm(500,log(100),0.5)  # Skewed to right
> x2<- rlnorm(500,log(100),0.5)  # Skewed to right
> mu<- exp(log(100)+0.5^2/2)  # mean of the log-normal distribution
> x2<- mu-(x2-mu)   # Skew this distribution to the left
> x<- c(x1,x2)    # Combine the two distributions
> plot(density(x))  # Check the result
> qqnorm(x)
> 
> 4.  from Rosenfeld, Simon (NCI) <rosenfes at mail.nih.gov> 
> 
> Zillion of methods: take for example student's t-distribution,
> cauchy or laplace
> 
> 5.  from Greg Snow <snow at fisher.byu.edu>
> 
> Take a look at the "rstab" function, it may be just what we want.
> 
> 6.  from David L Lorenz <lorenz at usgs.gov> 
> 
> His guess is that we want a distribution with positive 
> skewness.  The t
> distribution will do this.  Use the rt function to generate random 
> variates for any number of degrees of freedom.  The larger 
> the df, the 
> nearer normal.
> 
> 7.  from Matt Kurbat <Matt.Kurbat at kmv.com
> 
> We can use a mixture of normals distribution.  Our density will be a 
> weighted average of two normal densities (same mean, different 
> variances).  
> By varying the parameters of the normals, and the proportion allocated
> to each, we can achieve the desired result.
> Venables and Ripley (Modern Applied Statistics) discuss normal
> mixtures.
> 
> 8.  from jonathan david norton <jdnorton at midway.uchicago.edu> 
> 
> Generate normals, square them, put the original sign back  on. This
> distribution is symmetrical and has extremely heavy tails.
> 
> 9.  from Tom Jagger <tjagger at insightful.com> 
> 
> We can use the t distribution it has skewness and mean 0. 
> Use rt(n,df) where the degrees of freedom can be any positive real 
> number!
> 
> 10.  from Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU 
> 
> An easy way to do this is to use a mixture of two normal 
> distributions, 
> one of which has much bigger variance than the other, for example
> 
> y <- ifelse(runif(10000) < 0.95, rnorm(10000, sd = 1), 
> rnorm(10000, sd 
> = 5))
> 
> We can adjust the degree of kurtosis by adjusting either the mixture
> probabilies or the standard deviation of one of the components.
> 
> 11.  from Bob Wheeler <bwheeler at echip.com>
> 
> We can use the Johnson system. See the SuppDists package.

messages.subject: rmvnorm: non-pos.def. cov-mat (Summary)
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus Users,

Thanks to  C. Berry, T. Therneau, R. Gottardo, T. Hesterberg, and M. Kurbat
for their responses to my inquiry ("non-positive definite"
message from rmvnorm).  As my question may have betrayed, my linear
algerbra recollection could be better.

Several folks pointed out that a non-positive definite matrix actually
indicates an incorrect covariance matrix** although some suggested that IF
the violation (flagged by a negative eigen value)  was caused by a relatively
small negative eigen-value then the negative value may be an artifact of
numerical
error (i.e., "finite-precision floating point arithmetic") --- see Hesterberg
response below.

After checking my covariance matrix, I'm embarrased to say that it looks
suspect.
Further, the negative eigen-value is quite large.  So based on the responses
I believe the problem lies in my matrix.  It suggests an error in a previous
tabulation of that matrix --- something I will be following up upon.

The detailed responses were quite insightful, I've appended them below in case
others are interested.

Thanks again.

cheers,
Kevin

** Notably the interpretation in my original post was incorrect.
Negative eigen values, unless small enough to arise from numerical errors
(see Hesterberg response), indicate an improper covariance matrix.
A zero eigen value would indicate `collinearity', i.e., that
at least one of the rv's is a linear combination of a
subset of the remaining rv's.

====================

============== Charles C. Berry

You need a matrix square root.

If chol() chokes, try

x <- eigen(singular.symmetric.matrix)
sqrt.mat <- x$vectors %*% sqrt(diag(x$values)) %*% t(x$vectors)
k <- ncol(singular.symmetric.matrix)
res <- matrix( rnorm(n*k), nc=k) %*% sqrt.mat

var(res) should approximate singular.symmetric.matrix

if ncol(sing.mat) == 2, the plot of the resulting columns of 'res' should
be a line of dots whose slope is the ratio of the variances

If the number of zero eigenvalues is large, this will be inefficient.
Better to generate the full rank version in a subspace, then transform.
e.g. in two dimensions find the location on the (1 dimensional) line then
transform to two dimensional coordinates

You might need to check the eigenvalues for small negative values due to
roundoff errors.

Charles C. Berry                        (858) 534-2098
                                         Dept of Family/Preventive Medicine
E mailto:cberry at tajo.ucsd.edu          UC San Diego
http://hacuna.ucsd.edu/members/ccb.html  La Jolla, San Diego 92093-0645
====================

===================== Terry Therneau

 A multivariate normal distribution has, by definition, a symmetric positive
definite variance matrix.  Any SPD matrix has a cholesky decompostion.  Then,
your matrix must not be SPD.

  1. First case: you have a dependency.  For instance, there are 3 dimensions
in your distribution, but x3 = x1+ 3*x2. The variance matrix is non-negative
definite.
  2. Second case: not a variance matrix at all.  If the variance matrix is
not non-negative definite, then it can't be a variance matrix, since that would
imply that there exist random variables with negative variance.

     Terry Therneau
====================

==================== R. Gottardo

If you matrix is not non-positive definite, it does not mean that there is
colinearity.
It means that something is wrong. Covariance matrices are always positive
definite
(at least non-negative).  This is just a consequence of the definition of the
varaince Var(Y)>=0.

So to summarize if your matrix is not positive definite, YOU CAN NOT SAMPLE FROM
 IT.

Hope that helps,
Raphael
====================

====================== Tim Hesterberg

There are three cases to consider:
* covariance matrix has some negative eigenvalues
* covariance matrix has some zero eigenvalues
* covariance matrix has some zero eigenvalues, but numerical inaccuracy
  causes them to appear negative.

Case 1:
Negative eigenvalues should never in a covariance matrix.
rmvnorm() should stop, because you've made a mistake.
The relevant code is:
    eS <- eigen(cov, sym = T)
    if(any(eS$values < 0))
      stop("cov is not positive definite")

Case 2:
This should be fine; this is allowed.  The resulting random values
should fall in a linear subset of a higher-dimensional space.

Case 3:
When working with finite-precision floating point arithmetic,
eigenvalue or cholesky routines may calculate that there are negative
eigenvalues.  In this case you can just set the negative
eigenvalues to zero.

Check whether your negative eigenvalues are close enough to zero that
they could be due to roundoff error in numerical calculations, and that
the results you get with this approach are equivalent to setting
negative eigenvalues to zero.  If so you're fine.

I'll submit an enhancement request for a "tolerance" argument to
rmvnorm(), to allow some leeway in checking for negative eigenvalues.

Tim Hesterberg
====================

============= Mat Kurbatt

choleski is not defensible here.
lack of positive definitness here makes it fail because
(if i recall correctly - check a numerical computing book
to verify) it ends up requiring the square root of a negative
number.

one alternative is to perturb the covariance matrix
to make it positive definite (all eigenvalues positive).

hard to give a general purpose "alternative" method
because it depends on your problem.  one alternative
might be to use bootstrap resamples from the original
data as an alternative to having to using rmvnorm.

good luck,
matt
====================

=============ORIGINAL POST==============================

Dear Splus Users,

I am trying to randomly sample from a multivariate normal distribution whose
covariance matrix is apparently somewhat non-positive.  I understand that this
suggests some "collinearity" in a subset of the random variables, but don't
quite see why that would preclude a defensible random sampling procedure.
Applying rmvnorm causes a stop error owing to the non-positive matrix.  So on
the surface rmvnorm would not work for this case.

Some co-workers had previously sampled from this same multivariate normal
distribution using a Choleski decomposition approach.   I tried this same
approach and got the following warning when applying the Chol() function

     Warning messages:
       Warning in chol(covmat): Choleski decomposition not of full rank

I persevered and ignored this warning, completed the procedure to obtain a
result.   I worried that the result,
may not be defensible (given the warning ... which I'm unable to properly
interpret).  So my question is whether
the Choleski approach is defensible in this case.  And if not what is the
recommended approach is
(for sampling in the case of a non-positive covariance
matrix).

Thanks for any insight you can offer!
Kevin

==============

======================================+
Kevin P. Brand, Sc.D, MS
Research Associate
Dept. Epidemiology and Community Medicine
Faculty of Medicine
Univ. of Ottawa
Ottawa, Canada
Kbrand at uottawa.ca

Please address all correspondence to:
HECS-OPPS,

Ottawa, Ontario K1A 0L2

or glm model when the model.object is not available anymore; see original

messages.subject: Re: S4 classes and methods
messages.body_plain:
Ed Kademan wrote:
> 
> Matt Calder <calder at phz.com> writes:
> 
> >       I have a positive suggestion in regards to classes and object
> > oriented programming in S. It might be a slight overstatement, but I
> > believe the entire S object model could be based on a 'this' pointer
> > being available in all list objects. For example,
> >
> >       > x <- list(a=1, print = function() {cat('a = ', this$a, '\n')})
> >       > x$print()
> >         a = 1
> >       > x$a <- 4; x$print()
> >         a = 4
> >
> > [snip]
> 
> If S did have a standard and if that standard did not include these
> sorts of features that would not imply that you were forbidden from
> using them.  S is sufficiently powerful that you can implement
> language extensions yourself.  The following code goes a long
> way---maybe all the way---toward doing what the above describes.
> [snip]

Yes, there are some good applications for the Object Oriented
Programming model in S, and a start has already been made in exploring
how to do it.

There is a project, as part of Omegahat, to provide OOP-style classes
and methods for the S language.  It's still at an early stage, but
software and a little documentation is available on the omegahat web
site.  Go to the URL:
  http://www.omegahat.org/OOP
In particular, there is a draft there of an article on OOP software to
appear in the next issue of the R Newsletter.  The article is written
from the R viewpoint, but the software is provided in both R and S-Plus
versions.

OOP classes can be very useful in S.  But it's important to understand
that the computing model is quite different from that underlying most S
software.  (The R Newsletter article discusses the distinction.)  In
particular, S4 classes and OOP classes are quite different, and should
be.

The key to making OOP work in S is adding some notion of an object
reference, with the ability to change the object through the reference. 
The Omegahat OOP code does this, by two different mechanisms, for S-Plus
and for R.  (It's easier in R, where the notion of an environment is
close to that of a reference.)

We would very much welcome participation from others interested in
exploring OOP software in S.  The software is definitely not ready for
general use yet, but you can pick up the source from the omegahat web
site if you would like to experiment with it.

John Chambers

messages.body_plain:
Can anyone help me understand the following error observed under S-Plus 6 
(release 2) on Windows 2000?

A script (filename "caddy.ftgt.ssc") runs without error from an S-Plus 
script window.  However, trying to source it from the S+ command line gives 
a warning message:

> source("caddy.ftgt.ssc")
Warning messages:
    file "caddy.ftgt.ssc": incomplete last line in: parse(n = n, file = file)

The script is short, so I include the entire thing below:

---script starts below---
Caddy.Ftgt <- function(Flim=0.6,cvF=0.25,P=0.2)
{
        ### Computation of target reference point Fnow from limit reference
        ### point Fmsy, CV of current F estimate, and allowable probability
        ### of exceeding limit reference point
        ###
        ### Ref: Caddy and McGarvy 1996 NAJFM 16: 479

        c0 <- 2.515517
        c1 <- 0.802853
        c2 <- 0.010328
        d1 <- 1.432788
        d2 <- 0.189269
        d3 <- 0.001308

        t0 <- sqrt(log(1.0/P^2))

        denom <- 1.0 + cvF*(t0 - (c0 + c1*t0 + c2*t0^2)/(1.0 + d1*t0 + 
d2*t0^2 + d3*t0^3))

        round(Flim/denom,4)
}
---script ends above---

On Sun, 7 Oct 2001, Paul Y. Peng wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I used to create the DLLs in VC++6.0 by following the instructions
> in the Programmer's manual and defined DLL_LOAD during compilation.
> Recently, I tried to use a different name, say FILE_DLL instead
> of DLL_LOAD, in my c programs and the settings in VC++6.0.
> Surprisingly it doesn't work. I thought the name of the definition
> is irrelevant as long as there is one defined, just as it says
> that "DLL_LOAD was for the example only and not generally
> necessary" in p. 619 of the manual. One problem caused by a
> different name is that S_EVALUATOR is undeclared. I searched
> both S_EVALUATOR and DLL_LOAD in the include directories of
> S-PLUS and VC++6.0 and didn't find them. I must misunderstand
> the role of DLL_LOAD. Is it a must in making DLLs for s2000 if
> I use things like S_EVALUATOR in the DLLs? Thanks for shedding
> some light on this.

Well, S_EVALUATOR is for S4-based systems such as S-PLUS 5.x and 6.0,
and it is in the S-PLUS headers for those systems.  So I don't
know why you had problems on 2000, if you really have 2000.

The example on page 595 of the S+2000 Programmer's Guide using DLL_LOAD
uses it to add standard DLL startup code.  I've never found that necessary
in using any compiler to make DLLs for use with S-PLUS; any halfway-modern
compiler (even VC++6) generates suitable startup code if none is supplied.

The basic issue here is how exported variables are handled by Windows. You
can link to a function in an executable or in the same DLL or in another
DLL just by making sure it is extern, and for a DLL by using an import
library.  But *variables* in the same executable/DLL and those in another
are handled differently. So when you compile the code you need to know
which sort of linkage to make, and that's the defines are for, to get the
right declarations from the header files. (Well, smarter compilers than
VC++6 know how to do this automatically, but most don't and those that do
are not foolproof.)

However, my understanding (and as stated in S Programming) is that under
S-PLUS 2000 you need to define S_ENGINE_BUILD to get the non-DLL
convention, the another-DLL convention being the default.  That's on page
606 of the Programmers Guide.

--

messages.subject: lme with an incomplete design
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,

I have an experimental design with 1 blocking factor 
(random effect "seq", 6 levels) and 2 experimental 
factors (fixed effects, "SeqPos" and "dir", 
each having 4 levels) and 8 replications. 

For each sequence ("seq"), four observations have been successively made in
four different directions. The serial order is coded by "SeqPos" and the
direction by "dir". Each sequence was presented eight times in a randomized
order (I consider the sequences to be a random effect because they have been
arbitrarily selected among the set of all possible sequences of four
directions). For example, for sequences 6, the four directions presented were
2-0-4-6:
  
table(data$SeqPos[data$seq == 6], data$dir[data$seq == 6])
  0 2 4 6 
1 0 8 0 0
2 8 0 0 0
3 0 0 8 0
4 0 0 0 8

If one neglect the blocking factor (i.e. sequence), all directions
have been observed in all positions (though not the same number of times):
table(data$SeqPos, data$dir)
   0  2  4  6 
1 16  8 16  8
2  8 16  8 16
3  8 16  8 16
4 16  8 16  8

How would you analyze the SeqPos:dir interaction if you suspect that
the sequence (blocking factor) plays an important role? For example,

y.ijkl = mu + SeqPos.j + dir.k + SeqPos:dir.jk + seq.i + e.ijkl

can be fitted by 

lme(Targ=~SeqPos*dir, random=~1|seq, data=data)

However, the sequence position or direction might also have a different 
effect in each sequence in addition of their fixed effects. The model 
I have in mind is 

y.ijkl = mu + SeqPos.j + dir.k + SeqPos:dir.jk +           # fixed effects
                seq.i + seq:SeqPos.ij + seq:dir.ik + e.ijkl # random effects

Note that I do not allow for the triple interaction seq:SeqPos:dir.ijk
given the incompleteness of the design. What is the syntax for this
model? The following does not work:

lme(Targ=~SeqPos*dir, random=~1|seq/(SeqPos+dir), data=data)

Does this model make sense and what syntax should I use?

Given the design of the experiment, what alternative covariance 
stucture would you suggest that I try ? 

Any help would be appreciated

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

messages.subject: Re:
messages.body_plain:
There are three basic methods of handling a varying number of arguments.
Which is best depends on what you need to do.

1) give arguments default values:

        f <- function(x, y=NULL, z=NULL)
        {
           return( c(x,y,z) )
        }

2) check if arguments were given using missing():

        f <- function(x, y, z)
        {
           if( missing(y) && missing(z) )
                return( c(x) )
           else if( missing(z) )
                        return( c(x,y) )
               else
                return( c(x,y,z) )
        }

3) use "...", which means 'all other arguments' 

        f <- function(x, ...)
        {
           return( c(x,...) )
            }

messages.subject: Re: question on constraints in linear regression
messages.subject_clean: question on constraints in linear regression
messages.body_plain:
One possible approach is Tibshirani's "bootstrap
bumping" in which you bootstrap a few hundred model
fits and take the subset of these such that the coefficients
meet any constraints of interest.  This subset forms
the basis for getting standard errors of coefficient
estimates, etc.  The point estimates are from the
particular bootstrap resample that results in the
minimum sum of squared errors.  The bootcov function
in the Design library can help with part of this,
and its help file has a reference.  

One thing I like about this approach is that it provides
a poor person's Bayesian posterior probability that the
constraint is true (the proportion of resamples for
which the coefficients met the constraint).  -Frank Harrell

messages.subject: Power and CIs for noncentral F and chi-sq
messages.subject_clean: Power and CIs for noncentral F and chi-sq
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
   I've just joined the list and I noticed that not too far back there were
a couple of queries about quantiles for noncentral F, t, and chi-sq
distributions. I share an interest in this, since confidence intervals for
certain standardized effect size measures may be obtained via CIs for these
noncentrality parameters.
   I've written scripts (using S-Plus 2000 for Windows) that compute CI
limits for the noncentrality parameters for F and chi-sq, given an observed
chi-sq, df(s), and confidence level. I've also written one for finding the
noncentrality parameter value that ensures that power equals a requested
level, given alpha and the df(s). They just use bisection to home in on the
solutions. BTW, S-Plus's noncentral F calculator appears to be pretty
accurate even for large dfs and/or effect sizes (the same cannot be said
for Mathematica or SPSS). 
   If anyone's interested in having these bits of code, please email me.

Cheerio,
--Mike

S-users,

S+6 on Windows NT.  I have a function that does manipulate, mostly
categorizing continuous variables or redifining factors, a large data
frame.  The variables are manipulated through a for loop, at each pass it
prints the name of the variable getting manipulated.  Everything works fine
until it gets to this one variable "bmm", which is already a factor, we
just want to change the factor's names; this is done for several other
variables and works fine, but for "bmm" I get the following error message:

 Processing: assu3an
 Processing: priv
    .
    .
    .
 Processing: zone
 Processing: bmm
Problem in match.data.frame(x, table, nomatch, incom..: table must be a list 
the same length as x
Use traceback() to see the call stack

Strangly, if I process this variable at the top level there is no problem?

Here is a part of the function, it's pretty long and I don't want to make
you read too much code, hence I truncated it:

********************************************************************************
"PoFacLabels" <- function(dfr)
{
# Parameters:
#  dfr     : the input data frame.

  for (i in names(dfr))
    {cat(paste(' Processing: ', i, sep = ''), sep = '\n')
     switch(i,
### other variables processed.
           assu3an = dfr[, i] <- merge.levels(dfr[, i], k = list(
                            ' 0 = 0 - 3 an ' = c('0', '1', '2'),
                            ' 3 = 3 +   ans' = c('3', '4', '9'))),

                                                  ' 2 = central   ')),
### more variables processed
)
          }
  dfr
}
********************************************************************************

And here is the code I used to do the job at the command line.

********************************************************************************
ttt.bmm <- factor(inc.all[, 'bmm'], levels = c('B', 'ER', 'MA', 'MO', 'MT'),
                  labels = c(' Bon     ',

Can anyone shed some light on this?  It doesn't make sense to me that it works 
for other variables, being already factors as "bmm",

"bmm" within the function?

messages.subject: sum of vectors
messages.body_plain:
Dear all, 

My name is James Rizopoulos and I am a new S plus 2000
user for Windows

I have 50 vectors. Every vector has length 100. My
objective is to create the sum of these vectors

I found way of doing this:

For example if I had 4 vectors instead of 50  (My
objective is to create the sum: x1+x2+x3+x4)

x1 <- c(1:100)
x2 <- c(1:100)
x3 <- c(1:100)
x4 <- c(1:100)
out <- list(x1,x2,x3,x4)  
a <- numeric(100)
for(i in 0:100){
        si <- numeric(4)
        for(j in 0:3){
                y <- sum(out[[j+1]][i])
                si[j+1] <-  y
        }
        a[i+1] <- sum(si)
}
b <- replace(a, c(1), NA)
final <- a[!is.na(b)]
final

Is there any faster and easier way of doing this?

Thank you all for your help and for your time

=====
James Rizopoulos Undergraduate Student

Greece

PROTSIM     ACC=AXXXXXXXEEEE

messages.body_plain:
COURSE: Quantitative Financial Risk Management 
by Alexander McNeil
DATE: 1/2 November 2001
VENUE: Barbican Centre, London
http://www.uk.insightful.com/SPLUSMain/training/guru/mcneill.htm

Course Details:
This hands-on course will provide analysts and risk managers 
with a better understanding of quantitative tools for modern 
financial risk management. Whenever appropriate, theory 
will be illustrated by practical examples developed in the 
powerful S-PLUS environment, although prior familiarity 
with S-PLUS will not be assumed and the course may be 
followed by non-users of S-PLUS. The central technical issues 
are volatility, extremes, correlation, and the advanced 
statistical methods required to model these phenomena. 
Financial risk management confronts us with a real world 
of heavy-tailed risks, rapid changes and complex 
interdependencies which force us to go beyond standard 
statistical models and simplifying assumptions of normality 
to develop more sophisticated methodology. A basic knowledge 
of probability and statistics will be assumed. Concepts such as 
random variable, distribution, density, expectation, moments, 
parameter estimation and confidence intervals should be familiar 
to participants. No prior experience with S-PLUS will be assumed. 

Presenter Information:
Alexander McNeil is a Professor of Mathematics at the Swiss 
Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zurich. He completed 
a Ph.D. in mathematical statistics at Cambridge University in 
1993. He is interested in the development of sound statistical 
methods for financial risk management and his recent research 
has focused on extreme value theory (EVT), multivariate models 
for correlated risks, and credit risk methodology.
Alexander McNeil has held workshops on topics in quantitative 
risk management at international risk management conferences 
and also at actuarial summer schools hosted by Georgia State 
University and the Swiss Association of Actuaries. He is the 
author of the EVIS library of functions for extreme value analyses 
in S-PLUS and continues to develop S-PLUS libraries for risk 
management applications.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Brian,

At 09:18 PM 14/10/2001 -0500, Brian Beckage wrote:
> Hi everyone,
>
>
>
> I have a large design matrix (2465 rows by 26 columns) that is not full
> rank, i.e. when I use bic.logit(), which calls glim(), I get an error
> message to this effect.  The design matrix contains both continuous
> covariates and dummy variables.  A call to svd() yields:
>
> $d:
>  [1] 1.888973e+004 1.575508e+003 9.892808e+002 6.196773e+002 3.608400e+002
> 3.309583e+002 3.195417e+002
>  [8] 1.764203e+002 1.361555e+002 9.536627e+001 8.452058e+001 4.225352e+001
> 3.529728e+001 2.798886e+001
> [15] 2.123627e+001 1.427637e+001 9.525187e+000 7.205470e+000 2.879680e+000
> 1.709990e+000 8.257608e-001
> [22] 1.184660e-012 1.651152e-013 1.118988e-013 7.047769e-014 4.246685e-015
>
> which I interpret as meaning the rank of the matrix is 21 (because d[22:26]
> ~ 0).
>
> What is the easiest way to identify which columns of the design matrix are
> linearly dependent?

Take a look at the v matrix returned by svd, and examine the columns in v 
that correspond to the 0 entries in d. The nonzero entries in these columns 
of v correspond to the columns of the model matrix involved in each linear 
dependency.

messages.subject: Re: Random intercept in lme
messages.body_plain:
"Gary Kline" <gary_w_kline at hotmail.com> writes:

> I have problems specifying a 2-level linear mixed model. I have
> problems with is the intercept. For an example, lets use Equation 14.2
> on page 476 in Splus 6, Guide to Statistics vol.1 for Unix/Linux.
> (This is Equation 13.2 page 417, in statman1.pdf, accompanied with
> Splus2000 for PC)
> 
> I hope my use of full-stop to indicate subscript does not upset anyone
> The equation reads as follows:
> 
> d.ij = (Beta.00+Beta.01*sex.i+b.i0)+(Beta.10+Beta.11*sex.i+b.i1)age.j +E.ij
> 
> the text specifies to estimate the model as follows:
> 
> Fixed = distance ~ age  * Sex , random = ~ age

Be careful - the argument is called "fixed", not "Fixed" and S-PLUS is
case-sensitive. 

The formula "distance ~ age * Sex" in S-PLUS creates a model matrix
with a constant, the first-order terms for age and Sex and the
interaction.  Because Sex has two levels there will be a total of four
columns in the model matrix.  In your notation the columns correspond
to Beta.00, Beta.10, Beta.01, and Beta.11

> which makes perfect sense to me, except I cant see where the effect of
> sex on the intercept is accounted for.

It comes from the interaction term.  Remember that the '*' in an
S-PLUS formula specifies crossing of terms.

> If the data has the variable ?white?, a dummy for race, how
> would the following model be specified in Splus-lme language.

> d.ij =
> (Beta.00+Beta.01*white.i+b.i0)+(Beta.10+Beta.11*sex.i+b.i1)age.j +E.ij

fixed = white + age + age:sex, random = ~ age

It would be unusual to specify an interaction of age and Sex without a
main-effects term for Sex.  Depending on what age = 0 meant, this
model may not make sense because it would allow different slopes with
respect for age for the two sexes but require that they have the same
value when age = 0.

messages.subject: gls power

Many thanks to Prof. Brian Ripley for his prompt request related to gls
function varPower().
Also, I would like to thank Dr. Renaud Lancelot for his reference on the
book by Pinheiro & Bates. 
Solution is simple: in order to force varPower to use the known power pw I
have to write
varPower(fixed=pw) rather than varPower(value=pw). It works for me.

The original posting is below:

> Dear Colleagues:
> I am having problems with gls using varPower() function for modeling
> heteroscedasticity.
> I am estimating regression slope and its variance in two cases: when
> parameter value (power) in varPower is known
> and when it is not known. I can't see any differences in esimations AT
ALL.
> Looks like the function does not react on this parameter.
> I could understand this phenomenon if the parameter "value" is used as a
> first guess only. I think however that this is not the case:
> if I do not specify this parameter then gls should estimate it, if I
specify
> then gls should not estimate, just use it.
> I don't see any differences even if  the parameter value is completely
> wrong, for example is 100 instead of realistic 0.864.
> 
> Can anybody elucidate the situation?

Thank you

Simon Rosenfeld, 
NCI

Regarding the effect sizes in ANOVA, we received helpful emails from
Charles C. Berry, and Jarrett J. Barber. Their comments as well as my
original question follows. After going through some of the articles, we
decided not to do what we thought would be a "retrospective power
analysis". Since we already had the location or sample sizes that were
given to us a priori, and we had a large number of factors, as well as
continuous variables to evaluate, with different sample sizes
(locations) for each pair, we decided to report the sample size,
statistical significance, as well as a calculated effect size using the
formulas found in Cohen (1977).
We did finish this, but any more thoughts, and discussion on this matter
will be very welcome and I shall summarize.

Sincerely,

x[,v1]*x[,s1]+x[,v2]*x[,s2]+x[,v3]*x[,s3]

which takes less than a second.

Any recommendations, on how I can improve apply?

PS: To make things worse, some of the column contains NA's, so I need to
pass na.rm=T, which is much harder to do in straight summation.

Thanks,
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Replies:
-------------------------
Bill Dunlap:

apply(x, 1, sum) is calling sum() nrow(x) times and that takes
a while.  You can improve this a lot by using rowSums(), which I believe
we added for Splus 2000.  It is definitely in Splus 6.0.

In some cases the following psum() function is faster, but it doesn't
do any error checking (the all= argument must be a list: a data frame
is a list but a matrix is not).  You can call it as
        psum(all=data.frame(...), na.rm=T)
or
        psum(df[,1], df[,18], d[,92], na.rm=T)

psum <- function(..., na.rm = F, all = list(...))
{
        Sum <- rep(0, length(all[[1]]))
        for(el in all) {
                if(na.rm) {
                        el[is.na(el)] <- 0
                }
                Sum <- Sum + el
        }
        Sum
}

Now that rowSums is available psum is mainly a curiosity.
----------------------
Vadim Ogranovich:

Look at

Row and Column Summaries 

DESCRIPTION: 

Means, sums, or variances, by row or column. 

USAGE: 

colMeans(x, na.rm=F, dims=1) 
colSums(x, na.rm=F, dims=1) 
colVars(x, na.rm=F, dims=1, unbiased=T, SumSquares=F) 
colStdevs(x, na.rm=F, dims=1) 
rowMeans(x, na.rm=F, dims=1) 
rowSums(x, na.rm=F, dims=1) 
rowVars(x, na.rm=F, dims=1, unbiased=T, SumSquares=F) 
------------------------------
Biggerstaff, Brad J.:

I don't know if it'll be any faster than apply, but you might try

rowSums(x[,c(v1,v2,v3)]*x[,c(s1,s2,s3)],na.rm=T)

Brad
-----------------------------
Andrew Sinclair:
If summation is truly your goal, you could try matrix multiplication.
Not sure if it is actually quicker though.

e.g.

mat.to.sum <- x[,c(v1,v2,v3)]*x[,c(s1,s2,s3)]
mat.to.sum[is.na(mat.to.sum)] <- 0   ### remove NA's
ans <- mat.to.sum %*% matrix(1,nrow=3,ncol=1)

Regards,

Andrew

The 2002 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (IEEE ICDM '02)
provides a leading international forum for the sharing of original
research results and practical development experiences among
researchers and application developers from different data mining
related areas such as machine learning, automated scientific
discovery, statistics, pattern recognition, knowledge acquisition,
soft computing, databases and data warehousing, data visualization,
and knowledge-based systems.  The conference seeks solutions to
challenging problems facing the development of data mining systems,
and shapes future directions of research by promoting high quality,
novel and daring research findings.  As an important part of the
conference, the workshops program will focus on new research
challenges and initiatives.

Topics of Interest
==================

Topics related to the design, analysis and implementation of data
mining theory, systems and applications are of interest.  These
include, but are not limited to the following areas:

  - Foundations and principles of data mining 
  - Data mining algorithms and methods in traditional areas (such as
    classification, clustering, probabilistic modeling, and
    association analysis), and in new areas
  - Data and knowledge representation for data mining 
  - Modeling of structured, textual, temporal, spatial, multimedia and
    Web data to support data mining
  - Complexity, efficiency, and scalability issues in data mining
  - Data pre-processing, data reduction, feature selection and feature
    transformation

  - Soft computing (including neural networks, fuzzy logic,
    evolutionary computation, and rough sets) and uncertainty
    management for data mining
  - Integration of data warehousing, OLAP and data mining 
  - Man-machine interaction in data mining and visual data mining 
  - Artificial intelligence contributions to data mining 
  - High performance and distributed data mining 
  - Machine learning, pattern recognition and automated scientific
    discovery
  - Quality assessment and interestingness metrics of data mining
    results
  - Process centric data mining and models of data mining process 
  - Security and social impact of data mining 
  - Emerging data mining applications, such as electronic commerce,

messages.subject: Summary : Confidence intervals for logit
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The following solution provided by Ana Bio worked very well. Thanks Ana.
My original question follows at the end.

______________________________________________________________________
Hi Sarada,

Just use the prediction at the logit scale with the SE argument:

        predictionlogit <- predict(glm.object, type="l", se=T)

which gives you the prediction and SE on the logit scale.

With these you can calculate upper and lower 95% confidence limits using

        upperlogit <- predictionlogit$fit + 2 * predictionlogit$se.fit
        lowerlogit <- predictionlogit$fit - 2* predictionlogit$se.fit

and convert these to the response scale using

        upperresponse <- exp(upperlogit)/(1+exp(upperlogit))
        lowerresponse <- exp(lowerlogit)/(1+exp(lowerlogit))

The prediction on the response scale
predictionresponse <- predict(glm.object, type="r")
is obviously the same as
exp(predictionlogit$fit)/(1+exp(predictionlogit$fit))

Hope this helps

Best wishes,

Ana

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dear List,

is there any way that S-PLUS can provide confidence intervals for a
logit model, or can the deviance residuals reported by S-PLUS be used to
calculate 95% confidence intervals for the logit?   I used "predict.glm"
to get the logit and the predicted probabilities. However, I wish to
calculate the 95% confidence intervals on the logit and then transform
them into the probabilities, so that I can get 95% confidence intervals
for the calculated probabilities.

Any help will be greatly appreciated and I shall summarize.

Sincerely
Sarada Majumder
